newsitem.title: POLAND: Salomon sees Polish 97 C/A gap widening to $6 bln.
newsitem.headline: Salomon sees Polish 97 C/A gap widening to $6 bln.

text.p: Salomon Brothers in London expects the Polish current account deficit to widen to about $6 billion this year from $1.4 billion in 1996 and a $5.5 billion surplus in 1995, it said in a report.
Salomon analyst Miranda Xafa said in a market outlook dated March 6 that the shift reflected a rise in the Polish trade deficit to $8.2 billion in 1996 from $1.8 billion in 1995.
"The economic slowdown in Germany, Poland's biggest export market, has dampened export growth while domestic demand has picked up," the report said.

But despite the deterioration in the current account balance, capital inflows raised foreign exchange reserves by $3 billion in 1996 to $18 billion at end-December and Salomon expected those inflows to fully offset the 1997 current account gap.
"A deficit of this magnitude can easily be financed by capital inflows, but reserve accumulation could slow or reverse this year," the report said.

The Salomon analyst also saw the growing current account deficit reducing the probability that the authorities would soon opt for a cut in the rate of the crawling devaluation of the zloty, now at one percent a month.
"Such a move, which would increase the attractiveness of local currency instruments, is unlikely to happen in the next three to six months," she said.
The 1997 budget assumed that the rate of depreciation of the zloty's central rate would slow to nine percent in 1997 from the current 12.7 percent.
